io.title: std::io
io.summary: Input and output APIs, stream handles, formatted printing, scanning, and file operations.
overview: The std::io module provides the usual input and output tools through a Thrust interface. It keeps streams, files, printing, scanning, and small file helpers in one module, so basic I/O code stays easy to read.
Most functions call into std::ffi::c::io. That means the behavior is close to C stdio: return values should be checked, file handles must be closed, and formatting follows C-style format strings.

Use this module for terminal output, simple file access, buffered reads and writes, and cases where you need direct control over a stream. The API is low-level, but the names are clearer than calling the raw C bindings directly.
details: Formatted output uses variadic functions. Use print for stdout, printTo for a specific stream, and printToBuffer when the destination is a fixed-size buffer.
Reading and writing functions return the amount of data processed or a status code. Check those values instead of assuming the whole operation succeeded.
notes: Formatting helpers use C-style format strings, so the arguments must match the format.
closeFile must be called on successfully opened handles to release resources.
lockStream, tryLockStream, and unlockStream are available when a stream needs manual locking.

math.title: std::math
math.summary: Mathematical constants and wrappers around scalar math functions for f64 and f32.
overview: The std::math module gives Thrust names to common scalar math functions. It includes constants, trigonometry, logarithms, exponentials, rounding helpers, comparisons, and several special functions.
These functions are wrappers over the platform math library. You can write math::squareRoot or math::power in Thrust code without importing the raw C names everywhere.
For edge cases such as NaN, infinities, and domain errors, expect the same behavior as the C runtime on the target platform.
details: Use the exported constants, such as PI and TAU, instead of repeating numeric literals in formulas.
If a calculation calls expensive functions many times, store intermediate results yourself. The module does not hide that cost.
notes: Public constants are exported as f64 and intended for direct reuse.
Check inputs yourself when a function only accepts certain values.
Use std::math first. Drop to std::ffi::c::math only when you need the raw C function directly.

mem.title: std::mem
mem.summary: Allocation, reallocation, memory copy/move/set helpers, and memory mapping constants.
overview: The std::mem module contains raw memory operations. It covers allocation, reallocation, freeing, byte copying, byte moving, byte filling, comparison, and memory mapping constants.
The functions are direct by design. Sizes are byte counts, pointers are raw pointers, and ownership is managed by the caller.
Higher-level code, including vector, builds on this module. Use it when you need precise control over storage and are prepared to manage lifetimes explicitly.
details: Allocation functions can return nullptr. Always check the result before writing through the pointer.
Use moveMemory when the source and destination can overlap. Use copyMemory only when they are separate ranges.
notes: Lifetime ownership is manual. There is no automatic memory release.
All transfer helpers receive sizes in bytes.
Mapping constants are exposed to keep flag composition readable.

collections/vector.title: std::collections::vector
collections/vector.summary: Generic contiguous dynamic array with capacity growth and index-based operations.
overview: std::collections::vector is a generic dynamic array stored in contiguous memory. It stores a data pointer, a length, and a capacity.
The module exposes the usual operations: create a vector, push and pop values, remove values, access elements, iterate, reserve capacity, shrink storage, and drop the allocation when finished.
The API stays close to memory operations. This makes it useful for compiler data structures, parser buffers, and small tools where allocation behavior should stay visible.
details: Use newVector when you do not know the final size. Use withCapacity when you can reserve space up front.
Call dropVector when the vector is no longer needed. The vector owns heap memory once it grows or is created with capacity.
notes: Index-based helpers do not check bounds for you.
Pushing many values can grow the allocation. Reserve capacity first if you already know the size.
Write the element type at the call site when the compiler cannot infer it clearly.

tstring.title: std::tstring
tstring.summary: Owned null-terminated strings with byte operations, UTF-8 validation, and Unicode code point helpers.
overview: The std::tstring module provides TString, an owned string type implemented with std::collections::vector. It stores bytes as char values and keeps a trailing null terminator so the buffer can be exposed as a CString when needed.

Use TString when code needs a mutable string-like buffer with explicit lifetime management. The module covers construction from C strings, copying, concatenation, trimming, prefix and suffix checks, ASCII case conversion, and UTF-8 validation.

The API is still low-level. TString owns its vector allocation, so callers must destroy values they create when the string is no longer needed. Operations that return a new TString also return ownership to the caller.
details: len returns the byte length without the trailing null terminator, while capacity reports usable byte capacity without counting that terminator.
toCString returns a pointer to the internal null-terminated buffer. Treat that pointer as borrowed from the TString and avoid using it after the TString is destroyed or mutated.
get, hasIndex, and indexOf use byte indexes. get returns '\0' when the index is outside the string, and indexOf returns len(text) when the value is not found.
UTF-8 helpers also operate on byte indexes. isCharBoundary can be used before slicing-style logic, and decodeNext advances from one code point boundary to the next.
ASCII case conversion only changes bytes in the A-Z or a-z ranges. It does not perform locale-aware or full Unicode casing.
notes: TString values own heap storage through their internal vector. Call dropTString for every live TString when ownership ends.
Pointers returned by toCString are invalidated by destruction and may be affected by later mutations or reallocations.
Lengths and indexes are byte-based, not Unicode scalar counts. Use unicodeCodePointCount when you need the decoded code point count.
Use hasIndex before get when '\0' is also a valid value in the data you are inspecting.
Invalid UTF-8 decoding stops at the invalid byte and returns the current index from decodeNextData through the public decodeNext wrapper.
Version 0.2.2 adds string splitting, joining, searching, case conversion, and more Unicode decoding helpers.

ffi/c.title: std::ffi::c
ffi/c.summary: Type aliases, constants, and C ABI signatures used by standard wrappers.
overview: std::ffi::c contains the raw C bindings used by the standard library. The declarations are grouped by area, such as I/O, memory, math, and primitive C types.
Most application code should prefer std::io, std::mem, or std::math. Those modules use clearer Thrust names while still relying on the same C symbols underneath.
Use the raw FFI layer when you need a C symbol directly or when writing a wrapper for a library that is not yet covered by std.
details: Each declaration must match the external C symbol. Pay special attention to pointer types, return types, and variadic functions.
Keep raw extern calls in small wrappers when possible. That makes mistakes easier to find and keeps the rest of the program cleaner.
notes: Raw bindings follow the behavior of the C library on the target platform.
Prefer wrapper modules for normal application code.
When a C library changes, recheck the matching Thrust declarations.

optional.title: std::optional
optional.summary: Optional value container with presence checks and safe access.
overview: std::optional provides Optional[T], a container that may or may not hold a value. It represents an optional result without using null pointers.
Use some to wrap a value and none for absence. hasValue, isSome, and isNone report state, while unwrap returns the contained value and unwrapOr or valueOr give fallbacks.
details: Operations that return a new Optional transfer ownership to the caller, so the previous container no longer owns the value.
notes: Use isNone before unwrap when the value can be absent.
optional::Optional is also used by other containers such as vector::next.

env.title: std::env
env.summary: Process arguments, environment variables, and common system paths.
overview: std::env gives access to command-line arguments, environment variables, and platform directories such as the home and temporary directories.
hasArgument and argument read positional arguments; getVariable reads environment variables. Typed accessors such as argumentAsS32 and getVariableAsTString return ready-to-use views.
details: Use hasArgument and argument to inspect the command line, and getVariable or getVariableAsTString to read process environment variables by name.
Typed accessors such as argumentAsS32 and getVariableAsTString return converted values, so callers avoid re-parsing raw strings.
notes: Environment variable access can fail; check the result before using it.
Argument accessors are indexed starting from zero.

int.title: std::int
int.summary: Parsing of signed and unsigned integers from text.
overview: std::int parses integer values from C strings, TString values, and with explicit numeric bases.
parse[T] returns a result struct with the parsed value and a success flag. Variants such as parseWithBase and parseCString cover different inputs and bases.
details: parse[T] returns a result struct with a success flag, so callers can detect failures without exceptions.
Use parseWithBase for explicit numeric bases, and parseCString or parseTString when the source is a C string or TString.
notes: Check the success flag before reading the value.
Base variants accept bases from 2 to 36.

float.title: std::float
float.summary: Parsing of floating-point values from text.
overview: std::float parses floating-point values from C strings and TString values into f32, f80, or f64.
parse[T] returns a result struct with the parsed value and a success flag, mirroring the integer parsing helpers.
details: parse[T] returns a result struct with a success flag and supports f32, f80, and f64 targets.
Parsing follows C library rules for format and range; check the success flag before using the value.
notes: Check the success flag before reading the value.
Parsing follows the platform floating-point rules for the target.

random.title: std::random
overview: std::random produces pseudo-random unsigned integers and fills buffers with random bytes.
randomU64 and randomUsize return a random value, fillRandomBytes fills a buffer, and seedRandom seeds the generator.
details: randomU64 and randomUsize return unsigned pseudo-random values; fillRandomBytes fills a buffer in place.
Call seedRandom before generating values if reproducible output is required.
notes: This is not a cryptographic source of randomness.
Seed the generator when reproducible output is required.

collections/stack.title: std::collections::stack
overview: std::collections::stack is a generic LIFO container backed by contiguous storage.
push adds to the top, pop removes from the top, and peek reads the top without removing it. dropStack releases the storage.
details: push adds an element to the top; pop removes and returns the top element; peek reads it without removal.
Call dropStack when the stack is no longer needed to release the backing storage.
notes: peek and pop require a non-empty stack.
Reserve capacity when the maximum size is known.

collections/queue.title: std::collections::queue
overview: std::collections::queue is a generic FIFO container. enqueue adds at the back, dequeue removes from the front, and front or back read the ends without removing.
dropQueue releases the storage when the container is no longer needed.
details: enqueue adds at the back; dequeue removes from the front; front and back read the ends without removal.
Call dropQueue when the container is no longer needed to release the backing storage.
notes: dequeue requires a non-empty queue.
front and back read without removing the element.

collections/vecdeque.title: std::collections::vecdeque
collections/vecdeque.summary: Double-ended queue with push and pop on both ends.
overview: std::collections::vecdeque is a generic double-ended queue. It supports push and pop on both the front and the back.
pushFront, pushBack, popFront, and popBack operate on the ends; dropVecDeque releases the storage.
details: Operations are available on both ends: pushFront, pushBack, popFront, and popBack.
Call dropVecDeque when the container is no longer needed to release the backing storage.
notes: popFront and popBack require a non-empty deque.
Use this when you need efficient insertion and removal at both ends.

collections/hashmap.title: std::collections::hashmap
collections/hashmap.summary: Hash map from keys to values.
overview: std::collections::hashmap maps keys to values with insert, get, and remove.
get returns a pointer to the value or nullptr when the key is absent. insert returns true when the key was new. dropHashMap releases the storage.
details: get returns a pointer to the value or nullptr when the key is absent, so callers can test before dereferencing.
insert returns true when the key was new; dropHashMap releases the storage when the map is no longer needed.
notes: get returns a borrowed pointer; do not use it after the map is destroyed or rehashed.
Check the returned pointer for nullptr before dereferencing.

collections/hashset.title: std::collections::hashset
overview: std::collections::hashset stores a set of unique keys with insert, contains, and remove.
insert returns true when the key was new; dropHashSet releases the storage.
details: insert returns true when the key was new; contains reports presence; remove deletes a key.
Call dropHashSet when the set is no longer needed to release the backing storage.
notes: contains reports presence without removing the key.
insert returns true only for newly added keys.

intrinsics/int.title: std::intrinsics::int
intrinsics/int.summary: Integer intrinsics: overflow checks, saturation, and bit operations.
overview: std::intrinsics::int exposes low-level integer operations through intrinsic bindings: overflow-checked arithmetic, saturating arithmetic, and bit manipulations.
Use these when you need defined overflow behavior or direct bit operations not covered by the normal operators.
details: Overflow-checked and saturating arithmetic return a result struct with a value and an overflow flag.
Bit manipulation intrinsics map directly to LLVM instructions, so their behavior matches the target platform.
notes: These are primitive building blocks; wrap them in checked helpers for normal code.
Behavior follows the underlying platform integer instructions.

intrinsics/float.title: std::intrinsics::float
intrinsics/float.summary: Floating-point intrinsics: abs, min, max, sqrt, fused multiply-add.
overview: std::intrinsics::float exposes low-level floating-point operations through intrinsic bindings: absolute value, minimum, maximum, square root, and fused multiply-add.
Use these when you need precise control over floating-point behavior.
details: These intrinsics wrap LLVM floating-point operations such as abs, min, max, sqrt, and fma.
Use them when the normal operators do not expose the exact operation or rounding you need.
notes: These map closely to LLVM floating-point intrinsics.
Wrap them in helpers when used across many call sites.

ffi/c/env.title: std::ffi::c::env
ffi/c/env.summary: Raw C bindings for environment access.
overview: std::ffi::c::env exposes C environment functions such as getenv, setenv, unsetenv, and clearenv.
Prefer std::env for application code; use this layer when you need the raw C symbols directly.
details: These functions call directly into the platform C library environment helpers.
Prefer std::env unless you specifically need the raw C symbols.
notes: These follow the behavior of the C library on the target platform.
Calling setenv or unsetenv changes process-wide state.

ffi/c/int.title: std::ffi::c::int
ffi/c/int.summary: Raw C bindings for integer text conversion.
overview: std::ffi::c::int exposes C conversion functions such as atoi, strtol, strtoll, strtoul, and strtoull.
These return raw C results; check the end pointer or errno when conversion can fail.
details: The conversion functions return raw C results and may set errno on failure.
Check the end pointer or errno when a conversion can fail.
notes: Prefer std::int for safer parsing with result structs.
Follow the C semantics for overflow and invalid input.

ffi/c/float.title: std::ffi::c::float
ffi/c/float.summary: Raw C bindings for floating-point text conversion.
overview: std::ffi::c::float exposes C conversion functions such as atof, strtof, strtod, and strtold.
These return raw C results; check the end pointer or errno when conversion can fail.
details: The conversion functions return raw C results and may set errno on failure.
Check the end pointer or errno when a conversion can fail.
notes: Prefer std::float for safer parsing with result structs.
Follow the C semantics for overflow and invalid input.

ffi/c/random.title: std::ffi::c::random
ffi/c/random.summary: Raw C bindings for time and random numbers.
overview: std::ffi::c::random exposes C functions such as time, clock, rand, and srand.
These call directly into the platform C library.
details: These functions call directly into the platform C library.
Prefer std::random for application code unless you need the raw C symbols.
notes: This is the raw C layer; std::random offers a higher-level interface.
rand is not cryptographic and follows the C library behavior.

types.title: Types
types.summary: Primitive and built-in type forms used by Thrust.
overview: Thrust types are written explicitly. Integers, floats, pointers, arrays, function references, and void all appear directly in source code.
This makes declarations easy to read. When a function takes u32, ptr[s32], or array[char; 64], the size and shape of the value are visible at the call boundary.
Use concrete types in public APIs unless there is a clear reason to introduce a type alias or a generic parameter.
semantics: Fixed-width integers are best for public APIs and binary formats because their size is part of the name.
Pointers and arrays mean different things. A pointer refers to memory elsewhere, while an array type describes a sequence of elements.

reference_sections.title: Scalar Types
reference_sections.intro: Scalar values are stored directly and are usually passed by value.
items: Signed integers use the s prefix, such as s8, s16, s32, and s64. Use them when negative values are part of the domain.
Unsigned integers use the u prefix, such as u8, u16, u32, and u64. Use them for sizes, bit masks, and values that cannot be negative.
Floating-point values use f32 or f64 in normal code. Wider or target-specific forms include f80, f128, and fppc_128 (IBM PowerPC 128-bit).
bool represents true or false values. Keep boolean names descriptive because the type alone does not explain the condition.
char stores a byte-sized character value. Strings and UTF-8 data should still be treated as byte sequences unless a helper decodes code points.

reference_sections.title: Pointer and Array Types
reference_sections.intro: Pointer and array syntax makes memory shape visible at the use site.
items: ptr[T] points to a value of type T. The pointer may still be null or invalid, so code must check the value before dereferencing when the source is not trusted.
ptr[T, N] points to a value of type T in address space N.
ptr without a subtype is a raw pointer. Use it at FFI or allocator boundaries and cast back to a concrete pointer before reading typed values.
array[T] describes a dynamic array form. Its length is not part of the type.
array[T; N] describes a fixed-size array. The element count is part of the type and can be used by compile-time layout checks.
CString is the builtin alias used for null-terminated character arrays passed to C-style APIs.
Fn[param, ...] -> ret describes a function reference type. Use @arbitraryArgs to mark it variadic.

reference_sections.title: Aliases and Layout
reference_sections.intro: Aliases and layout builtins help keep public declarations readable without hiding representation.
items: type aliases give a name to an existing type. They do not create a separate runtime representation.
sizeOf, alignOf, and typeWidth report layout information known to the compiler. Use them for constants and static checks instead of repeating numeric assumptions.
ABI-oriented builtins such as abiSizeOf and abiAlignOf describe the representation required by the target ABI. Use them when interfacing with external code.

variables.title: Variables
variables.summary: Declaration and mutation patterns for local and static storage.
overview: Local variables are declared with var. You can write the type yourself or use := when the compiler can infer it from the initializer.
Static declarations store values for the lifetime of the program. They can also be marked public or bound to external names when needed.
Keep mutable variables close to the code that uses them. This makes loops and branches easier to follow.
semantics: Assignments change the current value of a variable. In longer functions, avoid spreading related assignments far apart.
Be careful with mutable static state. It is shared program state, so updates should happen through clear code paths.

reference_sections.title: Local Declarations
reference_sections.intro: Local variables live inside the block where they are declared.
items: var name: Type = value declares a local with an explicit type.
:= asks the compiler to infer the type from the initializer. Use it when the initializer already makes the type obvious.
A local declared in an inner block is not available after that block ends.
Mutation is explicit through assignment and compound assignment operators. Keep related mutations close together.

reference_sections.title: Static Storage
reference_sections.intro: Static declarations describe storage that exists for the lifetime of the program.
items: static values are module-level storage. They are useful for exported symbols, shared state, and data that must have a stable address.
static mut allows mutation of static storage. Treat it as shared state and keep writes in a small API.
@public exports a static symbol. @extern binds it to an external symbol name.

constants.title: Constants
constants.summary: Compile-time values that cannot be reassigned.
overview: Constants define values known at compile time. They are useful for sizes, flags, protocol values, and other numbers that should not be repeated throughout the code.
Constants can be built from compile-time helpers such as sizeOf and alignOf. That keeps layout-related values tied to the type they describe.
Use constants when the value is part of the program definition, not something that changes at runtime.
semantics: A constant cannot be reassigned. The compiler can use the value directly wherever the constant is referenced.
Keep constants near the code or module they describe. Very large global constant files are harder to maintain.

reference_sections.title: Compile-Time Values
reference_sections.intro: Constants are resolved while the program is compiled.
items: const name: Type = value declares a value that cannot be reassigned.
A constant expression can include literals and compile-time builtins such as sizeOf, alignOf, and pointerWidth.
Use constants for protocol values, flags, array sizes, ABI checks, and limits that are part of the program definition.

reference_sections.title: Constants Versus Variables
reference_sections.intro: Use constants when the value is a rule, not state.
items: A variable stores runtime state and can change as the function executes.
A constant documents a fixed decision and lets the compiler reuse that value directly.
If a value depends on input, file contents, allocation, or an external call, it belongs in runtime code instead of a const declaration.

functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Function declarations, arguments, return types, and visibility.
overview: Functions declare their parameters and return type in the signature. If no return type is written, the function returns void.
Attributes can be placed after the signature to export the function, bind it to an external symbol, or set a calling convention.
Write small functions with clear inputs and clear return behavior. This is especially important when a function owns memory or reports errors through status codes.
semantics: Use the return type to make the result clear. If a function can fail, choose a status code, nullable pointer, or another convention and use it consistently.
Put calling and linking attributes on functions that connect to outside code. Keep internal helpers simple.

reference_sections.title: Signature Parts
reference_sections.intro: A function signature states the name, parameters, return type, and optional attributes.
items: Parameters are written as name: Type and are checked at call sites.
The return type follows the parameter list. If omitted, the function returns void.
@public exports the function. @extern and @convention describe how the function connects to external symbols.
Named arguments can make call sites clearer when several parameters have the same type.

reference_sections.title: Return and Ownership Conventions
reference_sections.intro: The signature should make error and ownership behavior predictable.
items: Use status-code returns when a function can fail but does not produce a value.
Use nullptr or another documented sentinel when returning a pointer that may be absent.
If a function returns owned memory, document which function releases it and keep that convention consistent.

generics.title: Generics
generics.summary: Compile-time generic templates for functions and structures.
overview: Generics let one function or struct work with more than one type. The compiler creates concrete versions from the types used at call sites.
Type arguments are written in square brackets, such as add[s32](1, 2) or Vector[u8]. This keeps the chosen type visible.
Use generics for repeated patterns like containers or small helpers. Avoid using them when a concrete type would be clearer.
semantics: A generic instantiation behaves like ordinary concrete code after compilation.
Generic functions should make their assumptions obvious from the operations they use on T.

reference_sections.title: Instantiation
reference_sections.intro: Generic code is turned into concrete code for the types used by the program.
items: Function type arguments are written after the function name, for example add[s32](1, 2).
Struct type arguments are written after the struct name, for example Vector[u8].
Once instantiated, generic code follows the same type-checking and code generation rules as non-generic code.

reference_sections.title: Constraints by Use
reference_sections.intro: Current generic assumptions are expressed by the operations used inside the generic body.
items: If a generic function adds two values, each concrete T must support that operation.
If a generic container stores pointers or owns memory, document ownership at the API boundary.
Prefer concrete types when only one type is expected. Generics should remove duplication, not hide intent.

modules.title: Modules
modules.summary: Imports, aliases, and selective import scopes.
overview: Modules are brought into a file with import. A file can import a full module, give it an alias, or import only selected names.
Use selective imports when a file only needs a few symbols. This keeps the dependency list easier to scan.
Aliases are useful when a module path is long or repeated often.
semantics: Imports should show what the file actually depends on. Avoid importing large modules when one or two names are enough.
Use a consistent import style across nearby files so readers do not have to adjust to a new pattern each time.

reference_sections.title: Import Forms
reference_sections.intro: Imports control which external names are available in the current file.
items: import std::io brings a module into scope through its module path.
import "file.thrust" imports a source file by path.
as gives an imported module or file a shorter local name.
only limits the import to selected symbols. Use it when a file depends on a small part of another module.

reference_sections.title: Name Resolution
reference_sections.intro: Qualified names make module boundaries explicit.
items: Use module::symbol when a name comes from an imported module.
Aliases reduce repeated long paths but should still describe the imported code.
If two imports expose the same unqualified name, keep the access qualified instead of relying on reader memory.

statements.title: Statements
statements.summary: Conditional and control statements for runtime execution.
overview: Statements control what a function does step by step. Thrust uses explicit blocks for branches, loops, returns, and control statements.
Clear blocks make error handling easier to follow. They also make it easier to see where a function exits or changes state.
Prefer readable control flow over clever shortcuts, especially in code that handles pointers, files, or memory.
semantics: Use early returns for invalid input or error cases when that makes the main path clearer.
Avoid deeply nested conditionals when a small helper function would make the branch easier to understand.

reference_sections.title: Blocks and Branches
reference_sections.intro: Statements are grouped with braces so control flow is visible.
items: if and else select runtime paths based on boolean expressions.
A block creates a nested scope for local declarations.
return exits the current function. Code after an unconditional terminator is treated as unreachable by later checks.

reference_sections.title: Loop Control
reference_sections.intro: break and continue only make sense inside loops.
items: break exits the current loop.
continue skips the rest of the current iteration and proceeds with the next one.
breakAll and continueAll are broader loop-control forms. Keep them rare and close to the loop logic they affect.

compile-time-conditionals.title: Compile-Time Conditionals
overview: Compile-time conditionals choose code before the program is generated. The inactive branches are not emitted.
They are useful for platform-specific imports, constants, and declarations.
Use @if with target builtins such as isUnix, isLinux, or isWindows when a program needs different code for different targets.
semantics: Only the selected branch is kept. Each branch should still be valid for the target where it can be selected.
If many files need the same target decision, put that decision in one small module instead of repeating it everywhere.

reference_sections.title: Selection Time
reference_sections.intro: Compile-time conditionals are evaluated before code generation.
items: The selected branch remains in the program for that compilation target.
Inactive branches are not emitted, which allows target-specific declarations and imports.
Each branch should still be valid for the target where its predicate can become true.

reference_sections.title: Predicates
reference_sections.intro: Predicates usually come from target and compiler builtins.
items: Use target checks such as isUnix, isLinux, isWindows, isWasm, and pointerWidth for platform-dependent declarations.
Keep predicates small. Complex target rules are easier to maintain when moved into named constants or helper modules.
When a branch imports a platform file, test that branch on the matching target so it does not silently become stale.

attributes.title: Attributes
attributes.summary: Declaration modifiers for linkage, calling convention, and compile-time behavior.
overview: Attributes add extra instructions to a declaration. They can make a symbol public, bind it to a C name, change how a function is called, or give the compiler a code generation hint.
They are written next to the declaration they affect, so the rule is visible where the function, constant, static, struct, or enum is defined.
Most code only needs a few attributes, usually @public, @extern, @convention, @align, or @packed. Keep experimental attributes in narrow places where their purpose is clear.
semantics: Attribute order does not change what they mean, but using a consistent order makes declarations easier to read.
Be careful with @extern and @convention. They describe how Thrust code connects to external symbols, so changing them can break linking or calls into C code.
attribute_catalog: @public - exports the declaration with public visibility. Required alongside @extern.
@extern("symbol") - binds a declaration to an external symbol name.
@convention("name") - chooses calling convention, for example C, fast, Win64, or X86_64_SysV.
@linkage("kind") - sets LLVM linkage behavior. Accepted kinds include standard, common, dllimport, dllexport, externweak, weak, internal, linkerprivate, and linkerprivateweak.
@align(N) - sets explicit alignment in bytes (static/const/local contexts depending on declaration kind).
@heap - requests heap storage for local declarations.
@stack - requests stack storage for local declarations.
@packed - uses packed struct layout with reduced/removed padding.
@hot - marks a function as frequently executed.
@minSize - asks the compiler to prefer smaller generated code.
@inline - inline hint that allows the backend to inline when beneficial.
@noInline - prevents inlining of the function.
@alwaysInline - requests mandatory inlining at call sites.
@safeStack - recognized by the lexer, but the current attribute checker does not accept it on functions.
@weakStack - enables lighter stack protection mode.
@strongStack - enables stronger stack protection mode.
@preciseFloatingPoint - preserves strict floating-point behavior where supported.
@noUnwind - marks function as non-unwinding.
@noReturn - marks a function as non-returning. The compiler enforces a void return type and a terminating body.
@optFuzzing - marks a function for fuzzing-related compiler behavior.
@pure - recognized by the lexer, but the current attribute checker does not accept it on functions.
@thunk - marks function as thunk/trampoline style entry.
@constructor - runs at load/init stage and must be public.
@destructor - runs at unload/finalization stage and must be public.
@cuda - marks a function for a CUDA-oriented code generation path.
@asmSyntax("Intel"|"AT&T") - selects assembler syntax for asm functions (unstable).
@asmAlignStack - requests stack alignment for assembler function contexts (unstable).
@asmEffects - declares that assembler block has side effects (unstable).
@asmThrow - enables assembler error propagation behavior (unstable).
@promote(T1 -> T2, ...) - configures promotion map between types (unstable).
@arbitraryArgs - marks a function as variadic in user-facing syntax.
@if / @elif / @else - compile-time conditional directives (attribute-like syntax, handled in statement processing).
applicability_notes: For functions, the compiler accepts attributes for visibility, linking, calling convention, inlining, stack behavior, floating-point behavior, constructors, destructors, cuda, and promote.
Assembler functions also accept asm-specific attributes such as @asmSyntax, @asmAlignStack, @asmEffects, and @asmThrow.
Static and const declarations accept a narrower set: @public, @extern, @linkage, and @align.
Struct declarations accept @public and @packed. Enum declarations accept @public. Local declarations accept @heap and @align.

reference_sections.title: Linkage and Visibility
reference_sections.intro: Visibility attributes decide whether a symbol remains internal or is visible outside the module.
items: @public exports a declaration through the generated object file.
@extern binds a declaration to a symbol name that exists outside the normal Thrust name mangling path.
@linkage selects the LLVM linkage mode. Use non-standard linkage only when object-file or platform behavior requires it.

reference_sections.title: Calling and Code Generation
reference_sections.intro: Some attributes affect how a function is called or emitted by the backend.
items: @convention selects the calling convention. It must match the caller and callee across FFI boundaries.
Inlining and size attributes are backend hints or requirements. They should describe a specific need, not be applied everywhere.
@constructor and @destructor create load and unload hooks. Keep their bodies small and avoid hidden dependencies between them.

reference_sections.title: Layout and Storage
reference_sections.intro: Layout attributes should be tied to the data format or ABI that requires them.
items: @align(N) sets an explicit byte alignment where the declaration kind accepts it.
@packed changes struct padding. It can make field access less natural for the target, so use it for external layouts rather than normal data.
@heap requests heap storage for local declarations that need it. Keep ownership and destruction rules visible near the allocation.

builtins.title: Builtins
builtins.summary: Compiler-provided functions, low-level memory and ABI operations, and builtin types for type, target, host, and compile-time work.
overview: Builtins are compiler-provided functions and reserved operations. Some return information about types, some return information about the target or host, and some help validate assumptions while compiling.

They are often used in constants and static checks. For example, sizeOf(u32) can define a constant, staticAssert can stop compilation if an assumption is wrong, and target builtins can select one branch over another before code generation.
Use builtins when the value belongs to the compiler, the ABI, the target machine, or low-level memory operations rather than to ordinary runtime program state.
semantics: Compile-time builtins are evaluated while the compiler processes the program, and memory and ABI builtins lower directly to low-level memory operations, ABI queries, or compiler-managed variadic argument access.
When staticAssert or compileError fails, compilation stops immediately. Warnings produced by compileWarning continue compilation but still affect diagnostics output.

reference_sections.title: Type Layout Builtins
reference_sections.intro: These builtins describe the size and layout of a type as the compiler sees it.
items: sizeOf(Type) - returns the size of a type in bytes as usize.
alignOf(Type) - returns the memory alignment of a type as u32.
typeWidth(Type) - returns the bit width of a type as usize.
fieldCount(Type) - returns the number of fields in a struct type as usize.

reference_sections.title: Type Information Builtins
reference_sections.intro: These builtins answer structural questions about types.
items: fixedArraySize(Type) - returns the element count of a fixed-size array type as usize.
isSameType(A, B) - returns true when both types are exactly the same.
isPtrLike(Type) - returns true when the type is a pointer or another pointer-like type.
isFixedArrayOfSize(Type, N) - returns true when the type is a fixed array with exactly N elements.

reference_sections.title: Source Location Builtins
reference_sections.intro: These builtins expose the source position currently being compiled.
items: file() - returns the current source file as a constant string.
fileLine() - returns the current source line as u32.
currentFuncName() - returns the current function name as a constant string.

reference_sections.title: Compile-Time Check Builtins
reference_sections.intro: These builtins validate assumptions or emit diagnostics during compilation.
items: staticAssert(condition, "message") - stops compilation when the constant condition is false.
compileError("message") - always stops compilation with the given error message.
compileWarning("message") - emits a compile-time warning with the given message.

reference_sections.title: Compiler Information Builtins
reference_sections.intro: These builtins report facts about the compiler itself.
items: compilerVersion() - returns the compiler version as a constant string.
debugBuild() - returns true when the compiler itself is a debug build.

reference_sections.title: String Builtins
reference_sections.intro: These builtins operate on constant strings known to the compiler.
items: stringLength(string) - returns the length of a constant string as usize.

reference_sections.title: Type Predicate Builtins
reference_sections.intro: These builtins return booleans about general type categories.
items: isSigned(Type) - returns true when the type is a signed integer type.
isUnsigned(Type) - returns true when the type is an unsigned integer type.
isInteger(Type) - returns true when the type is any integer type.
isFloat(Type) - returns true when the type is a floating-point type.
isBool(Type) - returns true when the type is bool.
isChar(Type) - returns true when the type is char.
isPointer(Type) - returns true when the type is a pointer.
isArray(Type) - returns true when the type is an array form.
isFixedArray(Type) - returns true when the type is a fixed-size array.
isStruct(Type) - returns true when the type is a struct type.
isVoid(Type) - returns true when the type is void.
isConst(Type) - returns true when the type has const qualification.
isNumeric(Type) - returns true when the type is numeric.
isFunction(Type) - returns true when the type is a function reference type.

reference_sections.title: Target Information Builtins
reference_sections.intro: These builtins report what kind of machine and ABI the compiler is targeting.
items: targetOS() - returns the target operating system name as a constant string.
targetArch() - returns the target architecture name as a constant string.
targetVendor() - returns the target vendor name as a constant string.
targetAbi() - returns the target ABI name as a constant string.
targetTriple() - returns the full target triple as a constant string.
isLinux() - returns true when the target OS is Linux.
isWindows() - returns true when the target OS is Windows.
isDarwin() - returns true when the target OS is Darwin-based.
isApple() - returns true when the target vendor or platform is Apple-related.
isAix() - returns true when the target OS is AIX.
isUnix() - returns true when the target is a Unix-like platform (Linux, Darwin, BSD, Solaris/Illumos, AIX, or Haiku).
isBSD() - returns true when the target OS is a BSD derivative.
isFreeBSD() - returns true when the target OS is FreeBSD.
isNetBSD() - returns true when the target OS is NetBSD.
isOpenBSD() - returns true when the target OS is OpenBSD.
isAndroid() - returns true when the target OS is Android.
isIOS() - returns true when the target OS is iOS.
isSolaris() - returns true when the target OS is Solaris or Illumos.
isHaiku() - returns true when the target OS is Haiku.
is64Bit() - returns true when the target pointer width is 64 bits.
is32Bit() - returns true when the target pointer width is 32 bits.
isBigEndian() - returns true when the target byte order is big-endian.
isLittleEndian() - returns true when the target byte order is little-endian.
isX86() - returns true when the target architecture is x86.
isX8664() - returns true when the target architecture is x86_64.
isArm() - returns true when the target architecture is ARM.
isAarch64() - returns true when the target architecture is AArch64.
isRiscv64() - returns true when the target architecture is RISC-V 64-bit.
isPpc() - returns true when the target architecture is PowerPC.
isPpc64() - returns true when the target architecture is PowerPC 64-bit.
isMips64() - returns true when the target architecture is MIPS64.
isSystemz() - returns true when the target architecture is IBM System z.
isLoongarch64() - returns true when the target architecture is LoongArch64.
isWasm() - returns true when the target architecture is WebAssembly.
isWasm32() - returns true when the target architecture is WebAssembly 32-bit.
isWasm64() - returns true when the target architecture is WebAssembly 64-bit.
isElf() - returns true when the target object format is ELF.
isMachO() - returns true when the target object format is Mach-O.
isCoff() - returns true when the target object format is COFF.
hasPosixThreads() - returns true when the target environment supports POSIX threads.
hasSysvAbi() - returns true when the target follows the System V ABI family.
pointerWidth() - returns the target ptr width in bits as usize.
isizeWidth() - returns the target ssize width in bits as usize.
usizeWidth() - returns the target usize width in bits as usize.
pointerAlign() - returns the pointer alignment in bytes as usize.
maxAlignment() - returns the maximum supported alignment in bytes as usize.
targetCPU() - returns the target CPU name as a constant string.
targetCpuFeatures() - returns the enabled target CPU features as a constant string.
hasFeature("name") - returns true when the target CPU supports the named feature.

reference_sections.title: Atomic Builtins (Unstable)
reference_sections.intro: These builtins perform atomic read-modify-write and compare-and-swap operations. They require the compiler to run in unstable mode. The destination must be a variable declared with an atomic ordering modificator, and the operation inherits that ordering.
items: atomicStore(counter, value) - stores a new value and returns the previous one.
atomicAdd(counter, value) - atomic addition. The destination and value must be integers.
atomicSubtract(counter, value) - atomic subtraction.
atomicAnd(counter, value) - atomic bitwise and.
atomicNand(counter, value) - atomic bitwise nand.
atomicOr(counter, value) - atomic bitwise or.
atomicXor(counter, value) - atomic bitwise xor.
atomicSignedMaximum(counter, value) - atomic signed maximum.
atomicSignedMinimum(counter, value) - atomic signed minimum.
atomicUnsignedMaximum(counter, value) - atomic unsigned maximum.
atomicUnsignedMinimum(counter, value) - atomic unsigned minimum.
atomicCompareAndSwap(counter, expected, new, success, failure) - compares and swaps; returns true when the swap happened. expected is updated with the current value on failure.

reference_sections.title: Host Information Builtins
reference_sections.intro: These builtins report facts about the machine running the compiler, not the machine being targeted.
items: hostOsName() - returns the host operating system name as a constant string.
hostArch() - returns the host architecture name as a constant string.
hostEndian() - returns the host endianness as a constant string.
currentTimestamp() - returns the current host timestamp as usize.
processorCount() - returns the number of logical processors available to the host as usize.
hostName() - returns the host machine name as a constant string (CString).

reference_sections.title: Memory and ABI Builtins
reference_sections.intro: These builtins lower directly to low-level memory operations, ABI queries, or variadic argument access.
items: halloc(Type) - allocates heap memory for one value of the given type and returns ptr[Type].
memcpy(dst, src, size) - copies a block of memory and returns ptr.
memmove(dst, src, size) - moves a block of memory safely for overlapping ranges and returns ptr.
memset(dst, value, size) - fills a memory block with a byte value and returns ptr.
abiSizeOf(Type) - returns the ABI-defined size of a type in bytes as u64.
bitSizeOf(Type) - returns the size of a type in bits as u64.
abiAlignOf(Type) - returns the ABI-defined alignment of a type as u32.
arbitraryArgs() - returns the current variadic argument list as ptr.
arbitraryArg(Type) - reads one variadic argument of the given type.

reference_sections.title: Builtin Type
reference_sections.intro: The language also exposes one builtin alias that appears in many APIs.
items: CString - builtin alias for array[char], used for null-terminated string values.

reference_sections.title: Using Builtins in Declarations
reference_sections.intro: Builtins are most useful when they keep declarations tied to target facts.
items: Use sizeOf and alignOf to define capacities or layout checks that follow the referenced type.
Use target builtins to select platform-specific constants and imports through compile-time conditionals.
Use compileError and compileWarning for explicit diagnostics when a configuration is unsupported or unusual.

casts.title: Casts
casts.summary: Explicit type conversion between compatible source and target types.
overview: Casts convert a value to another type with as. They are useful when changing integer width, signedness, or pointer form.
Because casts are explicit, readers can see where a conversion happens instead of guessing which conversions the compiler inserted.
Use casts close to the boundary that needs them. If the rest of the function can use one clear type, prefer that.
semantics: Narrowing casts can lose information. Check ranges before converting to a smaller type.
Pointer casts should stay in low-level code where the memory layout is understood.

reference_sections.title: Numeric Casts
reference_sections.intro: Numeric casts are explicit because they can change representation.
items: Casting from a wider integer to a narrower integer can discard high bits.
Casting between signed and unsigned types changes how the same bits are interpreted.
Casting between integer and floating-point types can lose precision. Check ranges before relying on the result.

reference_sections.title: Pointer Casts
reference_sections.intro: Pointer casts should stay near code that knows the memory layout.
items: A raw ptr can be converted to a typed pointer when the pointed storage is known to hold that type.
A typed pointer can be converted to raw ptr for FFI and allocation APIs.
Do not use casts to bypass type errors in ordinary code. Prefer the correct type at the boundary.

loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: while, for, and loop constructs for repeated execution.
overview: Loops repeat a block while a condition holds, while a counter changes, or until the code breaks out explicitly.
In Thrust, loop state is usually visible in local variables. That makes it easy to see how the loop starts, changes, and stops.
Keep loops simple when they work with arrays or pointers. Small, direct loops are easier to check for off-by-one mistakes.
semantics: Use while when the condition is the main part of the loop. Use for when the initializer, condition, and step belong together. Use loop when the exit condition is inside the body.
Use break and continue sparingly. They are helpful, but too many exits make a loop harder to follow.

reference_sections.title: Loop Forms
reference_sections.intro: Use the loop form that matches where the exit condition lives.
items: while is best when the condition is checked before every iteration.
for keeps initializer, condition, step, and body together.
loop repeats until a break or return exits from inside the body.

reference_sections.title: State and Bounds
reference_sections.intro: Loop state should be visible and updated in one predictable place.
items: Keep counters and limits close to the loop header.
When indexing arrays or pointers, compare against the known length before the access.
Move invariant calculations before the loop to make the body easier to inspect.

structs.title: Structs
structs.summary: User-defined aggregate types with named fields.
overview: Structs group related fields under one type. Each field has a name and an explicit type.
They are useful for records, configuration values, handles, and small pieces of program state.
When a struct has rules about valid values, use helper functions to create or update it in one place.
semantics: Use field access to read or write named fields. If a field must stay consistent with another field, keep that update in a helper function.
For structs shared with C code, check field order and field sizes against the C definition.

reference_sections.title: Fields and Construction
reference_sections.intro: A struct value is built by naming each field and assigning a value.
items: Each field has its own explicit type in the struct declaration.
new StructName { ... } creates a value with the listed field values.
Use helper constructors when a struct has required defaults or related fields that must agree.

reference_sections.title: Layout and Interop
reference_sections.intro: Structs used across FFI boundaries need stable field expectations.
items: Field order matters when matching an external layout.
@packed changes padding behavior. Use it only when the external format requires it.
When a struct is shared with C code, verify field sizes and alignment with compile-time builtins.

enums.title: Enums
enums.summary: Named constants grouped under a common enum name.
overview: Enums group related named values under one name. In current Thrust, each member writes its type and value explicitly.
Members are accessed with the enum access operator, for example Mode=>Safe. The expression evaluates to the member value.
An enum name is not used as a variable type in the current compiler. Store the underlying value type, such as u32 or s32.
semantics: Treat the listed members as the expected values for that domain.
If those values must match an external format, keep that mapping in one place.

reference_sections.title: Members and Values
reference_sections.intro: Current enums are named groups of explicit constant values.
items: Each member writes its value type and concrete value.
Members are read with EnumName=>MemberName.
Store enum results in the underlying value type, such as u32 or s32.

reference_sections.title: Closed Domains
reference_sections.intro: Enums document the expected values for a small domain.
items: Use enums for modes, status codes, tags, and external numeric constants.
Keep values stable when they are part of a file format, ABI, or public API.
When behavior depends on every enum member, review all matches or condition chains after adding a member.

ffi.title: Foreign Function Interface
ffi.summary: Calling C functions through @extern and @convention attributes.
overview: FFI declarations let Thrust call functions provided by C libraries or the system. The declaration writes the Thrust signature, the external symbol name, and the calling convention.
These declarations are low-level. A good pattern is to keep them in one module and expose small wrapper functions to the rest of the program.
The signature must match the external function. Pay close attention to pointer types, strings, integer widths, and variadic arguments.
semantics: @extern gives the linked symbol name.
@convention("C") uses the normal C calling convention.

reference_sections.title: External Symbols
reference_sections.intro: FFI declarations describe symbols that are defined outside Thrust code.
items: @extern("name") gives the exact linked symbol name.
@convention("C") selects the C calling convention for calls across the boundary.
@arbitraryArgs marks variadic functions such as printf-style declarations.

reference_sections.title: Safety Boundary
reference_sections.intro: The compiler cannot verify that a C declaration matches the real C function.
items: Match integer widths, pointer types, return type, and variadic arguments exactly.
Keep raw declarations in one module and expose wrapper functions with clearer Thrust types.
Retest bindings when the target platform, C library, or header declaration changes.

deref.title: Deref and Pointers
deref.summary: Pointer access, references, and dereference operations.
overview: Pointers refer to memory by address. Dereference operations read or write the value stored at that address.
Because pointer mistakes are easy to make, Thrust keeps reference and dereference syntax visible in source.
Check pointers before dereferencing them, and keep raw pointer code small when possible.
semantics: Dereferencing nullptr or another invalid pointer is unsafe. Validate pointers before using them.
Pointer indexing should stay close to the code that knows the buffer size and layout.

reference_sections.title: References and Dereference
reference_sections.intro: ref and deref make address-taking and memory reads explicit.
items: ref value creates a pointer to storage that already exists.
deref pointer reads the value at the pointer location.
Writing through a pointer changes the storage reached by that pointer, not a copy.

reference_sections.title: Pointer Indexing
reference_sections.intro: Indexing a pointer or array relies on a valid base and a valid element offset.
items: Check for nullptr before dereferencing pointers from external code or allocation routines.
Keep the length or capacity used for bounds checks near the indexing code.
Use typed pointers when possible so the element type is visible at the access site.

variadic.title: Variadic Functions
variadic.summary: Functions that accept a variable number of arguments.
overview: A function marked with @arbitraryArgs accepts any number of extra arguments. The extra arguments are collected into a variable argument list that the body reads with the arbitraryArgs builtins.
The named parameters are declared as usual; the extra arguments are implicit. Callers can pass any number of them.
semantics: For variadic functions defined in Thrust without @extern, the compiler prepends a hidden usize argument with the number of extra arguments. Use arbitraryArgsCount to read it.
FFI variadic functions (@extern) keep the C ABI and do not carry the hidden count.

reference_sections.title: Reading Arguments
reference_sections.intro: The list is read with the arbitraryArgs builtins.
items: arbitraryArgs() returns the current variable argument list as ptr.
arbitraryArgFrom(list, T) reads the next argument of type T from list.
arbitraryArgsCopy(list) copies list so it can be read independently.
arbitraryArgsEnd(list) ends a list created with arbitraryArgsCopy or arbitraryArgsStart.
arbitraryArgsCount() returns the hidden argument count of the current variadic function.
arbitraryArgsStart() starts a new list for later use.

reference_sections.title: Supported Types
reference_sections.intro: arbitraryArgFrom only accepts scalar and pointer types.
items: Allowed types: integers, floats, pointers, bool, and char.
Reading a struct or array type is rejected; pass a pointer instead.

atomics.title: Atomic Operations
overview: The atomic builtins perform read-modify-write and compare-and-swap operations on a memory location. They map to the LLVM atomicrmw and cmpxchg instructions.
This feature is unstable. It only works when the compiler runs in unstable mode, and it can change or disappear.
semantics: The destination of an atomic operation must be a variable declared with an atomic ordering modificator, such as atomicRelax or atomicSync.
The operation inherits the ordering from the destination declaration. atomicNone and atomicFree do not describe an atomic operation and are rejected.
Compare-and-swap follows the C11 model: expected is passed by address and is updated with the current value on failure. The builtin returns true when the swap happened.

reference_sections.title: Read-Modify-Write Builtins
reference_sections.intro: Each builtin writes a value atomically and returns the previous value. The destination and value must be integers.
items: atomicStore(counter, value) - stores a new value, returns the previous one.
atomicAdd(counter, value) - addition.
atomicSubtract(counter, value) - subtraction.
atomicAnd(counter, value) - bitwise and.
atomicNand(counter, value) - bitwise nand.
atomicOr(counter, value) - bitwise or.
atomicXor(counter, value) - bitwise xor.
atomicSignedMaximum(counter, value) - signed maximum.
atomicSignedMinimum(counter, value) - signed minimum.
atomicUnsignedMaximum(counter, value) - unsigned maximum.
atomicUnsignedMinimum(counter, value) - unsigned minimum.

reference_sections.title: Compare-And-Swap
reference_sections.intro: atomicCompareAndSwap compares the destination against an expected value and swaps in a new value when they match.
items: atomicCompareAndSwap(counter, expected, new, success, failure)
expected is an lvalue holding the expected value; it is updated on failure.
success and failure are atomic ordering arguments using the atomic keyword literals.

assembler.title: Inline Assembler
overview: Assembler functions are written entirely in inline assembler. They support Intel and AT&T x86_64 assembler.
This feature is unstable. It only works when the compiler runs in unstable mode, and it can change or disappear.
semantics: An assembler function body has two blocks: the assembler lines and the constraints.
Assembler functions accept parameters, a return type, and attributes like normal functions.
The current asmfn parser expects assembler parameters as name Type without a colon. Assembler values (asm T { ... } { ... }) can carry attributes and typed arguments.

reference_sections.title: Related Attributes
reference_sections.intro: Assembler constructs use these unstable attributes.
items: @asmSyntax("Intel" | "AT&T") - selects the inline assembler syntax.
@asmAlignStack - aligns the stack for an assembler block.
@asmThrow - lets assembler errors propagate.
@asmEffects - tells the backend the assembler block has side effects.

reference_sections.title: LLVM Inline Assembler
reference_sections.intro: The assembler strings follow the LLVM inline assembler format.
items: See the LLVM language reference for the constraint and template syntax.
Assembler values can take attributes after the type and arguments inside parentheses after the type.
